report.answer_text:
Cause
AWS's post-event summary traced the outage to a latent race condition in DynamoDB's automated DNS management system[1]. It happened in the US-EAST-1 region in Northern Virginia. The automation left the DynamoDB address record empty, so anything trying to reach DynamoDB in that region couldn't find it.[2]
It was not a cyberattack. It was a fault inside AWS itself.[2]
How it unfolded
AWS puts the start at 11:48 PM Pacific on Sunday, October 19.[2]
DynamoDB was reachable again by 2:40 AM on Monday. Knock-on problems with launching servers and load balancers ran until 2:20 PM Pacific that afternoon.[2]
Those later problems came from dependent services. Services that depend on DynamoDB started failing too, including the system that launches new servers and the load balancers that spread traffic.[2]
Recovery was slow because systems had lost state. The cascade continued for hours after the root cause was fixed, and systems that lost state had to rebuild it.[1]
Afterward, AWS disabled the DNS Planner and Enactor automation worldwide while it added safeguards.[3]
What it disrupted
AWS services: The failure cascaded across core services such as EC2, Lambda, NLB, ECS/EKS, and dozens of downstream services.[4] Global features that depend on US-EAST-1 endpoints were also affected.
Amazon's own operations: Amazon.com itself went dark during the incident, along with numerous Amazon subsidiary services and even AWS customer support operations.[5]
Third-party apps and websites: Many downstream SaaS providers had outages too, with hundreds affected at once.[6] One source counted 6.5M Downdetector reports[7].
The search results didn't list individual consumer apps by name.
